nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It suggests modesty or timidity depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans find this word in formal writing, essays, and reviews. In everyday speech they usually say 'shy,' 'unsure of yourself,' or 'quiet.' It sounds polite and thoughtful when describing a person, but it can seem stiff if used in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Shy is the everyday word for timid around others; diffident is more formal and emphasizes a lack of confidence in one's abilities or opinions.
Humble is usually a positive trait of not boasting; diffident may describe hesitation even when someone is capable.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is pretty diffident, so he rarely asks for help with his yard.
examples.professional: Several engineers were too diffident to present their findings in the review.
examples.analytical: The author portrays the narrator as diffident, which allows the reader to observe his doubts without judgment.

nuance.analogy: Like a guest who stays near the door at a party instead of walking into the middle of the room.
nuance.etymology: From Latin diffidens, present participle of diffidere, to distrust.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'different' because of the similar first syllable.
Pronouncing it 'dih-FI-dent' with stress on the second syllable.
Using it as a noun instead of the noun 'diffidence'.

diffident.etymology: From Latin *diffīdentem*, present participle of *diffīdere* (“to mistrust”).

senses.definition: To invest with dignity or honor.
To give distinction to.
To exalt in rank.
To treat as worthy or acceptable; to indulge or condone by acknowledging.
senses.example: I will not dignify that comment with a response.

core.definition: To give someone or something dignity, honor, or respect, often making a simple thing seem more worthy.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, DIG. The middle syllable is a reduced nuh, and the last syllable rhymes with my.

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dignify in formal writing, speeches, and opinion pieces, usually when someone is given respect they did not previously receive. In everyday speech they would more likely say give it respect or make it seem important. It can sound stiff in casual talk, so keep it for formal or written contexts.

distinctions.note: Honor is common and can be a verb or noun, while dignify is more formal and emphasizes lending dignity to something.
Glorify means to praise or make something seem better than it is, often with an exaggerated tone; dignify is more restrained.

examples.everyday: Calling her a kitchen hero really dignifies the work she does every night at the shelter.
examples.professional: Naming the new program after the engineers dignifies the work they did and shows the company values their contributions.
examples.analytical: By treating the suffering of the poor as a subject for theology, the author seeks to dignify their experience and restore their place in the moral life of the church.

nuance.analogy: Like placing a plain wooden box on a velvet cloth in a museum, so people look at it with respect.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dignificare, from dignus, worthy, and facere, to make.
common_mistakes: Using dignify with a person as object without a clear reason, since it usually refers to actions or roles.
Confusing dignify with dignity, the noun.
patterns: not dignify sth with a response

dignify.etymology: From Old French *dignifier*, from Late Latin *dignificare*, from *dignus* (“worthy”) + *ficare*, *facere* (“to make”).

senses.definition: To have dinner away from one's house, usually at a restaurant.

core.definition: To eat dinner away from home, usually at a restaurant.

pronunciation.tip: Stress OUT, the second word, since it is a phrasal verb. The final t of 'out' is often flapped or lightly released, and the 'ow' sound is a diphthong.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests a pleasant outing, a treat, or a social occasion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dine out for going to a restaurant for dinner, especially for a special occasion or a night off from cooking. It is common in everyday speech: 'Let's dine out this weekend.' A natural reply is 'Sounds good, where do you want to go?' For a casual meal at lunch, people often say 'go out for lunch' instead.

distinctions.note: Eat out is the most common everyday phrase for eating at a restaurant at any meal; dine out often suggests a more formal or special dinner.
Go out to dinner is the most natural everyday phrase; dine out sounds slightly more polished or elegant.

collocations: dine out for a special occasion

examples.everyday: Our babysitter is free on Friday, so do you want to dine out with me for once?
examples.professional: After the project launch, the team decided to dine out together to celebrate our success.
examples.analytical: Economists have studied why households dine out more often as incomes rise, noting the shift from home production to purchased services.

nuance.analogy: Like taking a vacation for your kitchen, dining out gives you a night away from cooking and dishes.
nuance.etymology: From dine (from Old French disner) plus the adverb out.
common_mistakes: Saying 'dine out' when you mean to take food home; for that, say 'takeout' or 'to go.'
Stressing the first word, DINE out, instead of OUT in the phrasal verb.

conversation.text: We used to dine out every Friday night.
People dine out more around the holidays.
Do you dine out a lot, or do you cook at home?

senses.definition: To undo the integrity of; to break into parts.
To cause to break up into infinitesimal parts through the use of a disintegrator.
To fall apart; to break up into parts.

core.definition: To break into small pieces or fall apart, often gradually and completely.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on -SIN-, and the flapped t in 'intε' sounds like a quick d. The final -grate has the stress-free syllable grayt. Do not stress the last syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes breakdown, which may be physical, social or emotional.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disintegrate for physical objects, relationships, plans, economies and even people's composure, such as 'The old bridge began to disintegrate.' It is common in news and everyday talk about things falling apart. In casual speech 'fall apart' or 'come apart' is very frequent.

distinctions.note: Break down is informal and often used for machines or emotions; disintegrate suggests a more complete loss of structure.
Crumble suggests breaking into small pieces, often of something dry or solid; disintegrate can apply to abstract things too.

examples.everyday: The cookies left in the rain started to disintegrate into soggy crumbs.
examples.professional: Our release plan began to disintegrate once two key engineers left the project.
examples.analytical: Without shared norms, the community gradually disintegrates into rival factions.

nuance.analogy: Disintegrate is like a sandcastle when the tide comes in: the shape stays for a while, then the grains lose their hold on each other.
nuance.etymology: From dis- (apart) and integrate (make whole), from Latin integer (whole).
common_mistakes: Using 'disintegrate' with 'of' instead of 'into' when describing the result.
Stressing the last syllable: it is DIS-in-tuh-grayt, not dis-in-tuh-GRAYT.

senses.definition: To put out of place; to disarrange.
To move something, or someone, especially to forcibly move people from their homeland.
To supplant, or take the place of something or someone; to substitute.
To replace, on account of being superior to or more suitable than that which is being replaced.
senses.example: Electronic calculators soon displaced the older mechanical kind.

senses.definition: To have a weight equal to that of the water displaced.
To repress.

core.definition: To move something out of its usual place, or to force people to leave their home, or to take the place of someone or something.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, PLAYS, with a long a sound. The final s is a hard s, and the first syllable is a short i, not 'dee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use displace in news about refugees, disasters, and housing, and in workplace talk about a new person or technology taking over a role. In casual conversation they often say 'push out', 'move', or 'replace'. The word can sound slightly formal, so it fits best in writing and serious discussion.

distinctions.note: Replace is the everyday word for putting one thing in place of another, while displace can imply forcing something out of its place or position.
Dislodge means to remove something stuck or fixed in place; displace is broader and can describe people or roles.

examples.everyday: The new coffee machine kind of displaced the old one, so now nobody uses the french press.
examples.professional: Automated reporting has displaced some of the manual spreadsheet work, so the analysts are moving to modeling tasks.
examples.analytical: Heidegger's account of technology suggests that modern machines do not simply displace older tools but reframe how humans understand being.

nuance.analogy: Like a chair pushed out of its spot at a table, something displaced has lost its usual place.
nuance.etymology: From dis- 'apart' and place, from Latin locus 'place'.
common_mistakes: Using displace where replace is meant, as in 'displace the battery'; use replace for ordinary swapping.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the second.

senses.definition: The act of dissecting.
Something dissected. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
A minute and detailed examination or analysis.
Surgical removal.
senses.example: neck dissection

core.definition: The act of cutting an animal or plant apart to study its structure, or a detailed analysis of something into its parts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on SEK, the second syllable. The final -tion is pronounced shuhn, not tee-on.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In biology or medicine it is a neutral, scientific term; in criticism it can be a sharp or thorough analysis.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dissection most in biology, medicine and science classes, where students do lab dissections of frogs or fetal pigs. In a broader sense, a critic or journalist may say a detailed dissection of a policy or argument. In casual talk, people usually say 'breakdown' or 'analysis' instead.

distinctions.note: Analysis is the general word for studying something in detail; dissection suggests separating it into parts, often in a physical or very thorough way.
An autopsy is the examination of a dead body to find the cause of death; dissection is more general and can be used in biology labs.

collocations: a careful dissection of the argument

examples.everyday: My daughter had to do a frog dissection for biology class and came home very excited.
examples.professional: The consultant's dissection of the budget showed exactly where the overruns came from.
examples.analytical: Her dissection of the text separates its rhetorical strategies from its theological claims.

nuance.analogy: Like taking apart an old clock to see each gear, so you understand how the whole machine works.
nuance.etymology: From Latin dissecare, 'to cut apart', via dissectio.
common_mistakes: Using dissection as a verb; the verb is dissect.
Stressing the first syllable, saying DIS-ek-shun.

senses.definition: The Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox and Eastern Catholic eucharistic service.

core.definition: The principal Eucharistic worship service of Eastern Orthodox and Eastern Catholic Churches.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LIT in "liturgy," and the second word has a flapped or reduced "er." Say "dih-vine," not "dy-vine."

nuance.connotation: Neutral and religious; used respectfully within church contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "Divine Liturgy" in Orthodox and Eastern Catholic churches, and in discussions of worship. Western Christians often say "Mass" or "Communion service" instead. Within an Orthodox parish, people typically just say "Liturgy." Use the phrase with respect when talking to Orthodox believers.

distinctions.note: Mass is the Roman Catholic term for the Eucharistic service; Divine Liturgy is the Eastern Orthodox and Eastern Catholic term for the same central rite.
The Divine Liturgy is the Eucharistic service, while the Liturgy of the Hours is a cycle of daily prayers.

collocations: the Divine Liturgy of Saint John Chrysostom

examples.everyday: We're going to the Divine Liturgy at the Greek church this Sunday, so the kids can see the icons.
examples.professional: Our parish bulletin lists the Divine Liturgy at nine o'clock and vespers in the evening.
examples.analytical: The Divine Liturgy structures the believer's encounter with the Eucharist as participation in the heavenly worship described in Revelation.

nuance.analogy: The Divine Liturgy is like a home-cooked family dinner that has been prepared the same way for centuries: everyone knows the order, and the meal is the center of the gathering.
nuance.etymology: Liturgy comes from Greek leitourgia, "public service" or "work of the people"; divine is from Latin divinus.
common_mistakes: Calling it "Divine Mass" in an Orthodox setting, which many Orthodox Christians would find inaccurate.
Stressing the wrong syllable in liturgy as LI-tur-gy instead of LIT-er-jee.
Saying "dy-vine" with a long i in the first word.

senses.definition: The area of arrival and departure of a train in a railway station.

Any of the genus Rumex of coarse weedy plants with small green flowers related to buckwheat, especially bitter dock (Rumex obtusifolius), and used as potherbs and in folk medicine, especially in curing nettle rash.
A burdock plant, or the leaves of that plant.
The fleshy root of an animal's tail; specifically after clipping or cutting.
A leather case used to cover the clipped or cut tail of a horse.
A section of a hotel or restaurant.
senses.example: coffee dock

senses.definition: A device designed as a base for holding a connected portable appliance for providing the necessary electrical charge for its autonomy, or as a hardware extension for additional capabilities.
A toolbar that provides the user with a way of launching applications by their icons, and switching between running applications.
An act or instance of docking; joining two things together.
Ellipsis of scene-dock.
A fixed structure attached to shore to which a vessel is secured when in port; usually for loading and unloading.
Part of a courtroom where the accused sits.
To clip or cut off a section of an animal's tail; to practice a caudectomy.
To reduce (wages); to deduct from (someone).
senses.example: Her wages were docked by ten dollars.

senses.definition: To cut off, bar, or destroy.
senses.example: to dock an entail

senses.definition: To pierce holes, as pricking dough with a fork, to prevent excessive rising in the oven.
To land at a harbor.
To join two moving items.
senses.example: to dock spacecraft

senses.definition: To move a spaceship into its dock/berth under its own power.
In male homosexual sex, to engage in docking, the inserting of the tip of one participant's penis into the foreskin of the other participant.
To drag a user interface element (such as a toolbar) to a position on screen where it snaps into place.
To place (an electronic device) in its dock.
senses.example: I docked the laptop and allowed it to recharge for an hour.

core.definition: A platform built out over water where boats tie up, load, unload, or are repaired.

pronunciation.tip: Say a short, clipped vowel and a hard k at the end; do not add an extra vowel after the k. The vowel is the American ah sound, the same as in cot, so it does not sound like the British dok.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a dock is a practical, everyday place.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dock for the structure at a lake, marina, or harbor where boats are tied up. For a place where trucks load and unload cargo at a warehouse, they often say loading dock. Do not confuse it with the verb dock, which in everyday speech means to bring a boat or spacecraft alongside a structure.

distinctions.note: A pier is usually a longer structure built on pilings that extends from land, while a dock is often a smaller floating or fixed platform for boats.
A marina is a whole facility with many slips and services, while a dock is an individual landing structure.

examples.everyday: Can you help me tie the boat up at the dock before the wind picks up?
examples.professional: The shipping team said the container ship will dock at Pier 4 Thursday morning, so trucks need to be booked early.
examples.analytical: Engineers must check a dock's load capacity before approving a larger vessel for the harbor.

nuance.analogy: A dock is like a parking space for boats, a fixed spot where they can stop, rest, and get on and off.
nuance.etymology: Probably from Middle Dutch docke, a landing place or bed for ships.
common_mistakes: Using dock to mean a train platform, which is a platform or station in American English.
Confusing dock with dark or duck when pronouncing it, since the vowel is the short ah sound.

dock.etymology: From Middle English *dokke*, from Old English *docce*, from **dokkā*, from Proto-Germanic **dukkǭ* (compare, *dokkebladeren* (“coltsfoot, butterbur”)), from Proto-Indo-European **dʰew-* (“dark”).

conversation.text: The boat leaves from the dock at ten, so don't be late.
The kids love jumping off the dock into the lake.
The ferry should dock in about fifteen minutes.

senses.definition: The administration of a medication etc, in a measured amount; dosing.
The addition of a small measured amount of a substance to something, e.g. sugar to wine.
The measured amount so administered or added (the dose), combined with the frequency of administration and the time period for which it is taken.
senses.example: Why did he give you only a single 500 mg dose? The correct dosage of this antibiotic is one 500 mg tablet twice a day for 10 days.

core.definition: The amount of a medicine taken at one time, or how much is given over a period of time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final "-age" is a reduced, unstressed syllable that sounds like "ij," not "ahj" or "ayj."

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise, clinical word used in medical settings, and it is never insulting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "dosage" when talking about medicine, from pharmacists to doctors to ordinary patients. In everyday speech, people often say "dose" or "how much to take." Pharmacy labels usually say "take one tablet by mouth twice daily," and the word "dosage" appears on the instructions and in medical conversations.

distinctions.note: "Dose" is the single amount, while "dosage" can refer to the amount, the schedule, and the instructions together.
A "prescription" is the written order for a medicine, while "dosage" refers to how much and how often it is taken.

examples.everyday: Read the label carefully, because the dosage for children is different from the adult dosage.
examples.professional: The nurse confirmed the dosage with the pharmacy before giving the medicine to the patient.
examples.analytical: Determining the right dosage requires balancing therapeutic benefit against toxicity, which depends on body weight, kidney function, and time.

nuance.analogy: Dosage is like the recipe for a medicine: the ingredient is the same, but the amount and timing determine whether it helps.
nuance.etymology: From French dosage, from dose, from Greek dosis, "a giving."
common_mistakes: Using "dosage" to mean a single pill; "dose" is the more natural word for one amount.
Pronouncing the last syllable as "ahj" instead of a reduced "ij" sound.

conversation.text: Check the dosage on the box before you give it to the kids.
The doctor lowered my dosage because I was feeling dizzy.
Kids get a smaller dosage based on their weight.

senses.definition: A precipitous decline in fortune; death or rapid deterioration, as in status or wealth.
senses.example: Many economic and political reasons led to the downfall of the Roman Empire.

senses.definition: The cause of such a fall; a critical blow or error.
An act of falling down.
senses.example: a downfall of rain

senses.definition: To fall down; deteriorate; decline.

core.definition: A sudden loss of power, status, wealth, or success, or the cause of such a loss.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, DOWN, and keep the second syllable short and clear. Americans pronounce the final l clearly, so don't drop it.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a serious drop in fortune, reputation, or position, often caused by a mistake, scandal, or bad judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use downfall for both a person's ruin (a politician's downfall) and the thing that causes it (greed was his downfall). It is common in news, storytelling, and everyday talk about people or companies. To describe a sudden drop in prices or numbers, say drop or decline instead.

distinctions.note: Fall can be literal or figurative and neutral, while downfall usually refers to a final, serious ruin of someone's fortune or position.
Decline is a gradual decrease, whereas downfall suggests a more sudden and often complete collapse.

examples.everyday: Overconfidence was her downfall, and she lost the game in the last round.
examples.professional: The company's downfall came after it ignored warnings about its unreliable supply chain.
examples.analytical: Scripture presents pride as the root of a leader's downfall, linking inner disposition to outward ruin.

nuance.analogy: A downfall is like a building whose foundation cracks: the collapse seems sudden, but the damage was building for a long time.
nuance.etymology: From down plus fall, meaning a falling down.
common_mistakes: Writing 'downfal' with one l at the end.
Using downfall for a small, temporary drop, which is too strong; use setback or dip instead.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture links pride with ruin. Proverbs 16:18 (RSV) says pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall, so the downfall of the proud is treated as the natural result of their attitude. The Hebrew word for destruction, shever, appears in that verse, while fall is kishalon. Psalm 73:18-19 describes the wicked being brought to ruin suddenly, and Luke 14:11 says those who exalt themselves will be humbled.

senses.definition: A natural or artificial watercourse which drains a tract of land.
senses.example: ;;Saganing Drain, Vermuyden's Drain, the South Drain river, Najafgarh drain

senses.definition: A conduit allowing liquid to flow out of an otherwise contained volume; a plughole.
senses.example: The drain in the kitchen sink is clogged.

senses.definition: Something consuming resources and providing nothing in return.
senses.example: That rental property is a drain on our finances.

senses.definition: An act of urination.
One terminal of a field effect transistor (FET).
An outhole.
To lose liquid.
senses.example: The clogged sink drained slowly.

senses.definition: To flow gradually.
senses.example: The water of low ground drains off.

senses.definition: To cause liquid to flow out of.
senses.example: Please drain the sink. It’s full of dirty water.

senses.definition: To convert a perennially wet place into a dry one.
senses.example: They had to drain the swampy land before the parking lot could be built.

senses.definition: To deplete of energy or resources.
senses.example: The stress of this job is really draining me.

senses.definition: To draw off by degrees; to cause to flow gradually out or off; hence, to exhaust.
To fall off the bottom of the playfield.
To make a shot.

core.definition: To cause liquid to flow out of a container, sink, or area, or to empty it gradually.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is a diphthong, so say DRAYN, not 'dreen,' which is a common mistake. The flapped t doesn't apply here, but keep the r clearly rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the word is literal in most uses, and can be negative when describing energy or resources being used up.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say drain for sinks, bathtubs, and pools, and 'the drain' for the opening itself. In a kitchen or bathroom, 'Did you drain the pasta?' or 'The sink won't drain' are everyday phrases. For a person, 'That meeting drained me' means it left them exhausted.

distinctions.note: Empty describes a state of containing nothing; drain describes the process of removing the contents, often through an outlet.
Deplete is more formal and usually refers to supplies or resources running low; drain is more physical or concrete.

examples.everyday: Can you drain the pasta while I get the plates?
examples.professional: The new budget will drain our contingency fund by March, so we need to plan carefully.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that bureaucratic procedure drains public trust by making accountability invisible.

nuance.analogy: A drain is like a funnel that lets the water out of a bathtub, one drop at a time.
nuance.etymology: From Old English drēahnian, related to dry.
common_mistakes: Saying /dɹin/ (the vowel of 'green') instead of /dɹeɪn/ (the vowel of 'rain').
Using 'drain out' informally is fine, but 'drain the water' is more natural than 'drain the water out' in everyday speech.

conversation.text: Something is stuck in the shower drain.
Don't pour grease down the drain; it'll clog it.
Drain the pasta and add a little olive oil.

senses.definition: Leave a call early.

core.definition: To leave a phone or video call before it ends, or to be disconnected from it without meaning to.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on CALL, with a secondary stress on drop and off. The word the reduces to thuh before a consonant.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it usually describes a technical problem rather than rudeness.
nuance.usage_note: In work calls, Americans say I think I dropped off the call when their connection failed, or Sorry, I dropped off, can you repeat that? It is common in casual workplace talk. Nobody will think it is rude; a typical reply is No problem, I'll catch you up. It can also describe someone who had to leave a call early without saying goodbye.

distinctions.note: Hang up means ending a call on purpose; drop off the call often describes a disconnection nobody chose.
A dropped call is the noun for a call that ended by accident; drop off the call is the expression for what happens to the person.

collocations: lose the signal and drop off the call

examples.everyday: Sorry, my signal is bad, so I dropped off the call for a second.
examples.professional: Sorry, I dropped off the call, so could you recap the last action item?
examples.analytical: A video meeting makes it easy to drop off the call without anyone noticing, which changes how we track attendance.

nuance.analogy: It is like a car radio fading out in a tunnel: the signal is there one second and gone the next.
nuance.etymology: Built from drop off, meaning to fall away or leave, plus call; the expression is modern and tied to telephones.
common_mistakes: Saying drop from the call; the natural phrase is drop off the call.
Using it for a call you end on purpose, which is hang up.

conversation.text: I have to drop off the call early for another meeting.
Sorry, I dropped off the call when my Wi-Fi died.
Mark dropped off the call before we got to the budget.

senses.definition: Initialism of driving under the influence [of alcohol or other drugs]: the act of doing so; a charge or conviction for that act.
senses.example: DUI is punishable by jail time and by fines.

core.definition: Driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs, or a legal charge for it; abbreviation of this crime.

pronunciation.tip: Americans say the letters 'D', 'U', 'I' separately, so the word has three letter sounds. The main stress falls on the final letter 'I', which sounds like 'eye'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It refers to a serious crime with legal and insurance consequences.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'DUI' in everyday speech, news, and legal settings. Many people also say 'DWI' (driving while intoxicated), which is used in some states. It is widely understood, but it is a serious accusation, so avoid using it casually about someone's behavior.

distinctions.note: 'DWI' means driving while intoxicated, and some states use it for the same offense; 'DUI' is the more common term across the US.
'Drunk driving' is a general, spoken phrase; 'DUI' is the official abbreviation used in charges, records and legal writing.

examples.everyday: He got a DUI last year, so his car insurance went way up.
examples.professional: Our background screening flags any DUI within the past seven years for roles that require company driving.
examples.analytical: A DUI conviction signals risk, but a single record cannot fully predict future behavior, which complicates how such records are weighted in policy.

nuance.analogy: A DUI is like a bad mark on a permanent record: it follows you into insurance offices and job applications.
nuance.etymology: Initialism of driving under the influence, first used in the United States in the mid 20th century.
common_mistakes: Saying 'DUI' as one word like 'dwee,' when Americans say the letters separately as 'dee-yoo-eye'.
Using 'DUI' for driving while tired or distracted; it refers only to alcohol or drug impairment.

conversation.text: He got a DUI last year and lost his license for six months.
A DUI can cost you thousands of dollars in fines and lawyer fees.
Don't drink and drive; a DUI isn't worth it. Take a cab.

senses.definition: Manure; animal excrement.
A type of manure, as from a particular species or type of animal.
To fertilize with dung.
To release dung: to defecate.
To discard (especially rubbish); to chuck out.
To immerse or steep, as calico, in a bath of hot water containing cow dung, done to remove the superfluous mordant.

core.definition: Manure, or the waste matter that animals leave behind.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the short u of cut, and the final ng is a single nasal sound, not a separate g. Do not add a hard g at the end.

nuance.connotation: Negative and earthy. It is blunt and can be crude in conversation, though it is normal on farms and in the Bible.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dung mostly on farms, in gardening, and in agricultural or biblical contexts; in everyday talk, many people say manure instead, which sounds more polite. Calling something dung informally can mean something worthless or nonsense, which is a stronger, rude-sounding expression. Use it carefully in mixed company.

distinctions.note: Manure is the everyday, polite term for animal waste used as fertilizer; dung is more blunt and often more literary or biblical.
Feces is clinical or medical; dung refers to animal waste, usually in an agricultural or descriptive sense.

examples.everyday: My uncle uses cow dung in his garden because it helps the tomatoes grow.
examples.professional: Our agricultural report shows that composted dung improved soil nitrogen on the test plots.
examples.analytical: The prophet's use of dung as an image makes the humiliation of the people vivid and hard to ignore.

nuance.analogy: Dung is like the leftovers that feed the next crop: unpleasant on the surface, but it returns life to the soil.
nuance.etymology: From Old English dung, meaning manure, related to Old Norse dyngja, a dung heap.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long vowel as DOONG or with an extra g sound.
Using dung in polite conversation where manure would be expected.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible, dung usually refers to animal or human excrement, used as fertilizer or fuel, or as an image of shame, contempt, or worthlessness. The Hebrew word is often tzoah or related terms for dung, and the New Testament Greek word skybalon, in Philippians 3:8, is used by Paul to describe worldly gains as refuse. Ezekiel 4:12-15 describes the prophet being told to bake bread over human dung as a sign of the defilement of the people. 2 Kings 9:37 says the body of Jezebel will be like dung on the field, a picture of total disgrace.

dung.etymology: From Middle English *dung, dunge, donge*, from Old English *dung* (“dung; excrement; manure”), from **dungu*, from Proto-Germanic **dungō* (“dung”), from Proto-Indo-European **dʰengʰ-* (“to cover”).

senses.definition: The factorization of a matrix into a canonical form, whereby the matrix is represented in terms of its eigenvalues and eigenvectors.

core.definition: The factorization of a square matrix into its eigenvalues and eigenvectors, which expresses the matrix in a simpler diagonal form.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, EYE, with a secondary stress on 'dee'. The -tion ending is unstressed and sounds like 'shun'; the 'g' in eigen is hard, as in 'give'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; purely technical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eigendecomposition in linear algebra, numerical computing, machine learning, and statistics. In casual talk, engineers and data scientists usually shorten it to 'eigen decomposition' or 'the eigendecomposition' in meetings, or describe it as 'diagonalizing the matrix.' It is never an everyday word.

distinctions.note: Eigendecomposition applies only to square matrices and uses eigenvalues; SVD works for any matrix and uses singular values.
Factorization is the general idea of writing something as a product; eigendecomposition is one specific factorization.

examples.everyday: My coworker said the covariance matrix needs an eigendecomposition, and I just nodded.
examples.professional: We can speed up the model by precomputing the eigendecomposition of the kernel matrix once.
examples.analytical: The eigendecomposition of a diagonalizable matrix A gives A = VΛV⁻¹, which makes powers of A easy to compute.

nuance.analogy: An eigendecomposition is like finding the main axes of a stretched object: once you know them, the whole shape is simple to describe.
nuance.etymology: From German eigen, 'own, characteristic', plus decomposition from Latin decomponere, 'to separate into parts'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'eigen-DEE-composition' with the stress on the wrong syllable.
Assuming it works for any matrix; it requires a square matrix and is cleanest for diagonalizable ones.

senses.definition: The act or process of producing or refining with labor; improvement by successive operations; refinement.
The natural process of formation or assimilation, performed by the living organs in animals and vegetables, by which a crude substance is changed into something of a higher order.
senses.example: the elaboration of food into chyme

senses.definition: Setting up a hierarchy of calculated constants in a language such as Ada so that the values of one or more of them determine others further down in the hierarchy.

The process of taking a parsed tree of an abstract integrated circuit definition in a language such as Verilog and creating a hierarchy of module instances that ends with primitive (atomic) gates and statements.
The level of processing of a message or argument.

core.definition: The act of adding detail or developing an idea or process more fully; also, an added detail or refinement.

pronunciation.tip: Put the main stress on 'RAY', with a light secondary stress on 'lab'. The ending '-tion' is pronounced 'shun', and the middle 'er' is a reduced American r-colored vowel, not a full 'ear'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; positive when it describes helpful detail, negative when it implies unnecessary padding.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'elaboration' in academic writing, business, and technical contexts, such as asking for more elaboration in a meeting. In casual speech, people more often say 'more detail' or 'say more'. A polite request like 'Could you elaborate on that?' is very common and natural.

distinctions.note: An explanation makes something clear. An elaboration adds more detail to what is already said, which may or may not clarify.
Detail is a single specific fact. Elaboration is the process or result of expanding a point in depth.

examples.everyday: Could you give a bit more elaboration on why you're moving to Denver? I'm curious.
examples.professional: In the meeting, the director asked for more elaboration on the timeline before approving the budget.
examples.analytical: Her elaboration of the doctrine of grace draws on Augustine, but it also reworks his terms to address modern objections.

nuance.analogy: Like a sketch that becomes a finished painting through many added layers, an elaboration builds on a basic idea.
nuance.etymology: From Latin elaboratio, from elaborare ('to work out').
common_mistakes: Using 'elaboration of' where 'elaboration on' is more natural when discussing a topic.
Stressing the first syllable, 'EL-ab-or-AY-shun'; the main stress is on the '-ay' syllable.

core.definition: A man in the Bible who is one of Job's three friends and the first to speak in the debate about suffering in the book of Job.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, EL. The final syllable rhymes with jazz, not with ways.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in ordinary use. In Bible study it can carry the sense of a friend who gives confident but mistaken advice.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often hear this name in church or Bible study, usually in discussions of the book of Job. Calling someone an Eliphaz is a light joke in Christian circles about a friend who lectures without understanding. It is not common in casual speech.

examples.everyday: At Bible study, someone joked that the guy giving advice was being an Eliphaz.
examples.professional: When I teach Job, I start with Eliphaz because his first speech sets up the debate.
examples.analytical: Eliphaz argues that Job's suffering must reflect sin, and God later rebukes the friends for speaking falsely about him in Job 42.

nuance.analogy: Like a confident coworker who explains a problem without checking the data, Eliphaz speaks with conviction and gets the situation wrong.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in el-IH-faz.
Pronouncing the last syllable as fayz instead of faz.
nuance.biblical_note: Eliphaz the Temanite is one of Job's three friends who come to comfort him in the book of Job. His first speech appears in Job 4 and 5, where he argues that the innocent do not perish and that suffering follows sin. In Job 42:7 God says that Eliphaz and his friends have not spoken rightly of him, as Job has. The name is also borne by a son of Esau in Genesis 36:4.

senses.definition: A department of a hospital where seriously ill or injured patients, often with life-threatening conditions that require urgent or immediate treatment, are brought in, usually by ambulance.

core.definition: The part of a hospital that treats patients with urgent injuries or illnesses, often called the ER.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MUR in emergency and on ROOM in the compound. The word room is pronounced with a clear r and a long 'oo' vowel, so do not say 'rum'. In speech, Americans often shorten it to ER, pronounced as the letters E-R.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but it signals a serious or urgent situation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say emergency room or ER for the hospital department that handles urgent cases, and they say go to the ER in casual talk. Calling it the emergency department is more formal, and in the UK people say A&E or casualty. For minor problems, Americans often choose an urgent care clinic instead.

distinctions.note: Urgent care treats less serious problems and is cheaper; the emergency room is for life-threatening or severe conditions.
Hospital is the whole institution; emergency room is one department within it.

examples.everyday: My husband cut his hand badly, so we drove to the emergency room last night.
examples.professional: Please call the nurse line before sending anyone to the emergency room for that issue.
examples.analytical: The study compares emergency room outcomes for uninsured patients with those of patients who had regular primary care.

nuance.analogy: The emergency room is like a fire station for the body: it responds immediately when a crisis happens.
nuance.etymology: Emergency from Latin emergere, to rise out; room from Old English rum, space.
common_mistakes: Using the preposition 'in' with go or drive, as in 'go in emergency room'; the natural phrase is 'go to the emergency room'.
Dropping the article, saying 'go to emergency room'; American speakers normally use 'the' with emergency room.

conversation.text: They took him to the emergency room, but it was just a sprain.
We waited three hours in the emergency room.
The emergency room is for serious problems, not a cold.

senses.definition: To overwhelm.
senses.example: Depression engulfed her after her daughter's death.

senses.definition: To surround; to cover; to submerge.
senses.example: Only Noah and his family survived when the Flood engulfed the world.

senses.definition: To cast into a gulf.

core.definition: To cover or surround something completely, so that it is hidden or overwhelmed.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, and the 'ng' sound links into the 'g' with no extra vowel. Pronounce the final 'lf' as a clear 'f' with no separate 'l' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral; it often describes danger, emotion, or disaster overwhelming something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'engulf' often in news reports about fires, floods, and crowds, as in 'the fire engulfed the house.' In casual talk people may say 'swallowed up' or 'covered.' It can also be used for feelings, as in 'engulfed by fear.'

distinctions.note: Cover is neutral and general, while engulf implies a larger, more forceful surrounding that can overwhelm.
Overwhelm can describe feelings or tasks, while engulf is more physical and suggests being surrounded or swallowed.

examples.everyday: The kitchen was engulfed in smoke, so we opened every window.
examples.professional: The outage spread quickly and engulfed the whole billing system before we could isolate it.
examples.analytical: Doubt can engulf a believer's prayer, but it does not have to end in despair.

nuance.analogy: Engulfing is like a wave rolling over a sandcastle until nothing of its shape is visible.
nuance.etymology: From 'en-' (in) plus 'gulf,' from Old French 'golfe,' a whirlpool or abyss.
common_mistakes: Using 'engulf' for mild coverings, where 'cover' is more natural.
Saying 'engulfed with' instead of 'engulfed in' or 'engulfed by.'

senses.definition: The act of enrolling or the state of being enrolled.
The people enrolled, considered as a group.
The number of people enrolled.
The record of such enrolling; registration.

core.definition: The act of signing up for a school, program or plan, or the number of people who are signed up.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, roll, and the first vowel is a short i. The final -ment is weak, and the l is dark. The input transcription was wrong: the stress is on the root, not the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a practical, administrative word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use enrollment for schools, colleges and health insurance, as in open enrollment season. In schools, 'enrollment is up' usually means more students are registered. A natural reply to 'When is open enrollment?' is 'I think it starts in November.'

distinctions.note: Registration is a general sign-up step; enrollment often refers to a formal ongoing membership in a school or plan.
Attendance is who actually shows up; enrollment is who is officially registered.

examples.everyday: Open enrollment for our health plan starts next month, so check your options.
examples.professional: Enrollment in the data science certificate has doubled since last year.
examples.analytical: Enrollment figures alone cannot show whether students are learning, since they measure access rather than outcomes.

nuance.analogy: Like a roster on a sports team, listing who is officially part of the group.
nuance.etymology: From enroll plus the suffix -ment.
common_mistakes: Using enrollment for attendance; attendance is who actually comes.
Pronouncing the first syllable as en instead of in.

senses.definition: To put on the throne in a formal installation ceremony called enthronement, equivalent to (and often combined with) coronation or other ceremonies of investiture.
senses.example: ceremonially enthrone

senses.definition: To help a candidate to the succession of a monarchy (as a kingmaker does), or by extension in any other major organization.
To exalt, to praise.
senses.example: The novel seemed to enthrone love as the highest virtue.

core.definition: To place a king, bishop, or other leader on a throne in a formal ceremony, or to honor someone with a position of great authority.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, THROHN. The th is voiceless, and the vowel is a long o diphthong ending in n.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes an official honor or elevation, and it can be used to praise someone's rise to prominence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use enthrone in everyday talk. It appears in news about royal or church ceremonies abroad and in religious or literary writing about God or rulers. In a casual setting, people would say crown, install, or put in charge.

distinctions.note: Crown focuses on placing a crown on a ruler's head, while enthrone focuses on seating someone on the throne in a formal installation.
Install is a general word for placing someone in a job or office, while enthrone is formal and suggests a ceremonial, elevated position.
Exalt means to praise or raise in honor, while enthrone specifically means to seat someone in a position of authority.

examples.everyday: I saw on the news that the new king will be enthroned next month in a big ceremony.
examples.professional: The board will enthrone the new chief executive at the annual meeting, though the formal title will not take effect until July.
examples.analytical: In Psalm 47 the poet presents God as the one who is enthroned over the nations, so political power is measured against divine authority.

nuance.analogy: To enthrone someone is like placing the final piece of a crown on a carved statue, marking the moment it becomes the center of attention.
nuance.etymology: From en- (in, on) and throne, from Greek thronos (seat, chair), meaning to place on a seat of honor.
common_mistakes: Using enthrone for ordinary appointments, such as enthroning someone as team lead, which sounds too formal.
Confusing enthrone with dethrone, which means removing someone from power.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible the Hebrew verb yashab (to sit, dwell, be enthroned) and the noun kisse (throne) describe God as seated in authority over creation and Israel. Psalm 22:3 says God is enthroned upon the praises of Israel, linking worship with God's presence. Psalm 47:8 teaches that God reigns over the nations and sits upon his holy throne. Psalm 9:7 says the Lord sits enthroned forever, emphasizing God's eternal and just rule.

senses.definition: The right to have something.
A person's perceived but unjustified right to something; a tendency to claim what one does not deserve.
Power, an authority to do something.
Something to which one is entitled.
A legal obligation on a government to make payments to a person, business, or unit of government that meets the criteria set in law, such as social security in the US.

core.definition: A legal right to a benefit or privilege, or a belief that one deserves special treatment without earning it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TY, the second syllable. The IPA you were given starts with a schwa, but Americans usually begin with a clear IN sound, and the last syllable is reduced to mint.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in policy and law, such as Social Security or Medicare entitlements. Negative when describing a person's attitude, as in a sense of entitlement.
nuance.usage_note: In American politics and news, entitlements means government programs like Social Security and Medicare, and it is used neutrally. When describing a person who expects special treatment, Americans say a sense of entitlement, which is often critical. Use it carefully at work, since calling a colleague entitled can sound like an insult.

distinctions.note: A right is a basic freedom or claim, while an entitlement is a specific benefit provided under a law, plan, or contract.
Privilege describes an advantage given by status or birth, while entitlement describes a claim to it, often one the person has not earned.

examples.everyday: My uncle says the younger generation has too much of a sense of entitlement.
examples.professional: Our health plan covers the benefit as an entitlement under the employee contract.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the rhetoric of entitlement obscures the difference between earned claims and unearned privileges.

nuance.analogy: An entitlement is like a ticket that was given to you by a rule, or that you believe you should have been given.
nuance.etymology: From entitle plus the suffix -ment, from Old French and Latin roots meaning to give a title or name to.
common_mistakes: Using entitlement to mean simply a right in every context, when Americans often mean a specific benefit or an unearned claim.
Stressing the last syllable instead of the second.

senses.definition: The great circle midway between the celestial poles; the celestial equator.
An equinoctial gale.
(rare) The terrestrial equator.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: Of or relating to the spring or autumnal equinox.
senses.example: an equinoctial gale or storm, i.e. one happening at or near the time of the equinox, in any part of the world

senses.definition: Of or relating to the celestial equator.
Of flowers: that open and close at particular times of day.
(uncommon) Equatorial: of or relating to the equator of the Earth.
senses.label: uncommon

core.definition: Relating to an equinox, when day and night are roughly equal in length.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on NOK, with the short ah-like American vowel as in knock. The -tial ending is pronounced as shuhl, and the final syllable is weak.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds scientific or poetic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use equinoctial mainly in astronomy, sailing or literary writing. In everyday speech people say spring equinox or autumn equinox, or just the day when day and night are equal. The word can sound overly formal in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Equinoctial refers to the equinox or the celestial equator; equatorial refers to the Earth's equator or regions near it.

examples.everyday: My grandmother always said the end of March was the time when the days finally start getting longer.
examples.professional: The telescope schedule was set around the equinoctial period, when the sun crosses the celestial equator.
examples.analytical: The ancient calendar anchored the festival to the equinoctial date, when day and night were nearly equal.

nuance.analogy: Like a day that sits exactly at the midpoint of a seesaw between light and dark.
nuance.etymology: From Latin aequinoctialis, from aequinoctium (equal night), from aequus (equal) and nox (night).
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as putting the main stress on the final -al.
Dropping the t in the middle, writing equinocial.

equinoctial.etymology: Middle English *equinoctial*, *equinoccial*, *equinoxial*, from Old French *equinoxial*, from Latin *aequinoctiālis*, from *aequinoctium* + *-alis*.

senses.definition: An example.
A story demonstrating a moral point; a parable.

core.definition: A short story or example used to teach a moral lesson, such as a parable or fable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, ZEM. The final -um is a reduced, weak syllable close to uhm, not oom. The word is Latin in origin but Americans say it in English style.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a technical term from literary and religious history.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exemplum mainly in literary criticism, medieval studies, and religious history. Ordinary speakers would say parable, fable, or moral story. You will mostly meet it in academic reading about medieval sermons.

distinctions.note: A parable is a story from the Bible or a religious teaching; an exemplum is a broader medieval genre of moral anecdote, often used in sermons.
A fable usually has animal characters and a clear moral; an exemplum may use human characters and is more closely tied to preaching.

examples.everyday: My friend who teaches medieval literature said the story my grandmother told was basically an exemplum about not lying.
examples.professional: The sermon collection includes a dozen exempla that the preachers could adapt for their congregations.
examples.analytical: Chaucer's Pardoner's Tale draws on the exemplum tradition, using a cautionary story to expose hypocrisy.

nuance.analogy: Like a short case study in a business book, told to make one lesson memorable.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exemplum, example or model.
common_mistakes: Using exemplum as a generic word for example in ordinary English.
Pluralizing it as exemplums; the Latin plural exempla is common in scholarly writing.

senses.definition: Suitable to effect some desired end or the purpose intended.
senses.example: Most people, faced with a decision, will choose the most expedient option.

senses.definition: Affording short-term benefit, often at the expense of the long-term.
Governed by self-interest, often short-term self-interest.
A method or means for achieving a particular result, especially when direct or efficient; a resource.

core.definition: Useful and practical for achieving a particular result quickly, even if it is not the best long-term choice.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on spee. The final -ent is a reduced syllable, so it sounds like "unt," not "ent" with a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use expedient as an adjective in formal or professional contexts, such as "the expedient solution." In casual speech they would say "quick," "easy," or "the simplest way." Used with a negative tone, it suggests that the choice was made for convenience rather than principle.

distinctions.note: Convenient describes something easy or comfortable to use, while expedient emphasizes that something is practical for getting a result.
Efficient focuses on using resources well, while expedient focuses on being practical in a particular situation, even if it wastes resources.

examples.everyday: Taking the highway is expedient today, since the side streets are closed for the parade.
examples.professional: Given the deadline, it is expedient to reuse the existing code rather than rewrite the module.
examples.analytical: An expedient compromise can resolve a dispute immediately, but it may leave the underlying disagreement unaddressed.

nuance.analogy: An expedient choice is the key that opens the door fastest, even if it is not the one that fits the lock best over the years.
nuance.etymology: From Latin expedire, "to free the feet, extricate," from ex- and pes, pedis, "foot."
common_mistakes: Using expedient to mean fast in general; it means practical for a purpose.
Placing the stress on the last syllable, as in ex-pe-dee-ENT.
patterns: it is expedient (for sb) to do sth

expedient.etymology: From Middle English *expedient*, from Old French *expedient*, from Latin *expediens*, present participle of *expedire* (“to bring forward, to dispatch, to expedite; impers.

senses.definition: In the nature of exploitation; acting to exploit someone or something.
senses.example: We are protesting the company's exploitative policies.

senses.definition: Of or relating to exploitation.
Wherein one organism reduces a resource to the point of affecting other organisms.

core.definition: Taking unfair advantage of people, especially to gain money or power from their work, need or vulnerability.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SPLOY. The middle syllable '-ta-' is reduced to 'tuh', and the ending is 'tiv', not 'teev'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it criticizes unfair treatment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'exploitative' in news, labor debates and business criticism, such as 'exploitative lending' or 'exploitative wages'. It is more formal than 'unfair' and less common in casual speech, where people say 'that's a rip-off' instead.

distinctions.note: Predatory suggests deliberately targeting victims, often in lending or crime; exploitative describes unfair use of people's labor or need more generally.
Exploratory means investigating or testing; it has no negative sense and is a different word.

examples.everyday: That phone plan is exploitative; they keep charging me extra fees for nothing.
examples.professional: Legal flagged several clauses in the vendor contract as exploitative toward our smaller partners.
examples.analytical: Dependency theorists argued that trade relations between core and peripheral economies were structurally exploitative.

nuance.analogy: An exploitative arrangement is like a landlord who keeps the rent high because the tenants have nowhere else to go.
nuance.etymology: Formed from exploit with the suffix -ative, from Old French esploit, ultimately from Latin explicitum.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'exploratory' because the words look similar.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'ek-splo-TAY-tiv'.

senses.definition: A trust or confidence in the intentions or abilities of a person, object, or ideal from prior empirical evidence.
senses.example: The faithfulness of Old Faithful gives us faith in it.

senses.definition: A conviction about abstractions, ideas, or beliefs, without empirical evidence, experience, or observation.
senses.example: I have faith that my prayers will be answered.

senses.definition: A religious or spiritual belief system.
senses.example: The Christian faith.

senses.definition: An obligation of loyalty or fidelity and the observance of such an obligation.
senses.example: He acted in good faith to restore broken diplomatic ties after defeating the incumbent.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of by my faith.

core.definition: Strong trust or confidence in someone or something, or a religion; in Christian theology, trust in God and his promises, especially in Christ.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable that rhymes with 'wraith.' The 'th' is voiceless: put the tongue between the teeth and blow air, instead of saying 'fate' or 'faith' with a 't' or 's.'

nuance.connotation: Generally positive, meaning trust and loyalty. 'Blind faith' is negative, and 'bad faith' implies dishonesty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'faith' for religious belief ('people of faith'), for trust in a person ('I have faith in you'), and for a religion ('the Jewish faith'). 'Faith-based' describes organizations tied to religion. It is polite and widely understood, though some people avoid it in work settings.

distinctions.note: Belief is accepting something as true; faith adds trust and commitment.
Trust is reliance on a person or thing; faith is stronger and often goes beyond evidence.
Confidence is usually based on evidence or experience, while faith may go beyond it.
Religion is an organized system of belief and practice, while faith is personal trust or belief.

examples.everyday: I know the interview was tough, but I have faith in you.
examples.professional: We signed the agreement in good faith, expecting both sides to honor it.
examples.analytical: For Paul, faith is not mere intellectual assent but trust in Christ that transforms the whole person.

nuance.analogy: Faith is like sitting down in a chair without testing it first: trust shown by action.
nuance.etymology: From Old French feid, from Latin fides 'trust, belief.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'th' as 't' ('fate') or 's' ('face').
Saying 'faith on' or 'faith to' instead of 'faith in' someone or something.
Treating it as countable when it means trust: 'a faith' means a religion, but 'faith' alone is trust.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek pistis means trust, belief and faithfulness, and the Hebrew emunah means firmness or reliability. Hebrews 11:1 describes faith as assurance of things hoped for. Romans 10:17 says faith comes from hearing the message about Christ. James 2:17 says faith without works is dead.

traditions.view: Faith is trusting participation in God's life, expressed in worship, sacraments and the faith of the Church. It cannot be separated from love and action.
Faith is a theological virtue, a gift of God by which one believes what he has revealed. It works through charity and is held with the Church's teaching.
Faith is trust in Christ and the sole means of receiving justification. Reformed and Lutheran traditions call it God's gift, while Baptists and evangelicals stress personal decision and trust.

faith.etymology: From Middle English *feith* (also *fay*), borrowed from Old French *foi*, from Latin *fidēs*.

senses.definition: Feverish, or having a high temperature.
Full of nervous energy.
Involving fever as a symptom or cause.

core.definition: Having a fever or a high body temperature; feverish. It can also describe something involving fever as a symptom.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is reduced to 'bruhl'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, since it describes illness. It is mostly clinical.
nuance.usage_note: Doctors and nurses use febrile in medical notes, such as febrile patient or febrile illness. Ordinary Americans say feverish or have a fever. Using febrile for a fever in casual talk sounds overly clinical. Figurative use for nervous energy is literary and uncommon.

distinctions.note: Feverish is the everyday word used by most Americans; febrile is more technical and clinical.

examples.everyday: The kid felt hot and was febrile all night, so we called the pediatrician in the morning.
examples.professional: The nurse flagged the patient as febrile and asked the team to order blood cultures.
examples.analytical: The essay treats the febrile political climate of the period as a symptom of deeper anxieties.

nuance.analogy: A febrile body is a thermometer reading too high, the way a febrile mood is an emotional temperature that runs too hot.
nuance.etymology: From Latin febrilis, from febris (fever).
common_mistakes: Saying FEE-brile with the stress on the second syllable.
Using febrile as a casual synonym for excited without understanding its clinical tone.

febrile.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin *febrīlis*, from Latin *febris* (“fever”).

senses.definition: The act of fixing.
The state of being fixed or fixated.
The act of uniting chemically with a solid substance or in a solid form; reduction to a non-volatile condition; -- said of volatile elements.
The act or process of ceasing to be fluid and becoming firm.
In metals, a state of resistance to evaporation or volatilization by heat.
A state of mind involving obsession with a particular person, idea, or thing.
A sexual fetish or turn-on.
Recording a creative work in a medium of expression for more than a transitory duration, thereby satisfying the "fixation" requirement for the purposes of copyright law.
senses.example: In order to obtain copyright on a recording in the United States, the recording must have been reduced to fixation on or after February 15, 1972.

senses.definition: The change in a gene pool from a situation where there exists at least two variants of a particular gene (allele) to a situation where only one of the alleles remains.
Process by which an injury is rendered immobile.
Maintaining of the gaze on a single location (either momentarily or prolongedly).
Preservation of biological tissues from decay due to autolysis or putrefaction.

core.definition: An intense, persistent focus on one idea, person or thing, often to an unhealthy degree, sometimes called an obsession.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable '-say'. The ending '-tion' is pronounced /ʃən/, like 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. In everyday talk it usually describes an unhealthy or excessive preoccupation, though it can be neutral in a psychological context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fixation' in psychology and in casual talk to describe an unhealthy obsession, such as 'He has a fixation on his fantasy football stats.' It is slightly more clinical than 'obsession'. In technical fields such as chemistry it has separate meanings, so specify the context if you need precision.

distinctions.note: 'Obsession' is the more common everyday word; 'fixation' is more clinical and often used in psychology.
'Interest' is positive or neutral; 'fixation' implies the focus is excessive and hard to shake off.

examples.everyday: My roommate has a fixation with cleaning the kitchen every night.
examples.professional: Our manager has a fixation on quarterly numbers, which distracts the team from long-term goals.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the nation's fixation on economic growth obscures questions of meaning and justice.

nuance.analogy: Like a magnet that holds a needle in one spot, a fixation keeps the mind pulled toward one object.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin 'fixatio', from 'fixare', 'to fix'.
common_mistakes: Using 'fixation' with 'of' rather than 'on'; the usual preposition is 'on' (a fixation on something).
Confusing 'fixation' with 'fixture' or 'fixing', which have different meanings.

senses.definition: Becoming tired or less dynamic; declining in strength; dwindling.
A pavement or sidewalk of flagstones; flagstones, collectively.
The process by which something flags or tires.
The skewing or bending of the upper part of a television picture due to imperfect synchronization of the video signal.
Use of a handkerchief code or analogous display to signal sexual interests.

core.definition: Becoming tired, weaker, or less energetic; losing strength or momentum over time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The -ing ending is a reduced, unstressed syllable, and the g is a hard sound, as in 'go'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative; it describes a gradual decline in energy, interest, or performance without implying disaster.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'flagging' mostly for energy, enthusiasm, or sales, as in 'flagging energy' or 'flagging interest'. It often appears in news about economies, markets, or sports teams. In casual speech people more often say 'running out of steam' or 'slowing down'.

distinctions.note: 'Tired' describes a person's state after exertion; 'flagging' describes a gradual decline in something's strength or interest over time.
'Declining' is more neutral and can describe a long, measurable trend; 'flagging' suggests a loss of energy or spirit.

examples.everyday: Around 4 p.m. my energy starts flagging, so I grab a coffee.
examples.professional: Our quarterly sales are flagging, so we need to rethink the pricing strategy.
examples.analytical: Her argument grows more flagging in its final pages, as the evidence thins while the claims grow bolder.

nuance.analogy: A flag on a pole that droops when the wind dies down.
nuance.etymology: From the verb 'flag,' meaning to droop or lose strength, probably of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Using 'flagging' for a physical flag that is folded or hanging; it describes loss of strength, not a cloth banner.
Confusing the stress; the first syllable is strong, so avoid 'fla-GING'.

senses.definition: Untried or inexperienced.
Emergent or rising.
A young bird which has just developed its flight feathers (notably wings).
An insect that has just fledged, i.e. undergone its final moult to become an adult or imago.
An immature, naïve or inexperienced person.

core.definition: New to a field and not yet experienced or confident; still developing, as a fledgling business or fledgling democracy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The letters "dge" are pronounced like the "j" in "judge", and the second syllable is a reduced "-ling" with no strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly positive; it suggests promise and early stage rather than failure, though it can imply someone is not yet trusted.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for new companies, teams, artists or people starting a career, often in news writing or business talk. It is slightly literary, so in casual speech people might say "new" or "just starting out" instead. Calling a person a fledgling can sound patronizing if said to their face.

distinctions.note: A novice is simply a beginner in a skill; fledgling emphasizes that something is newly formed and still vulnerable.
Emerging is more neutral and business-like, while fledgling adds a sense of fragility or youthful inexperience.

examples.everyday: My daughter is a fledgling guitar player, so the living room is pretty noisy these days.
examples.professional: We are supporting a fledgling data team that only started building our forecasting models last quarter.
examples.analytical: The fledgling state lacked the institutions needed to sustain its constitutional commitments during its first decade.

nuance.analogy: Like a baby bird that has just grown its first flight feathers: ready to try, but not yet strong enough to fly far.
nuance.etymology: From fledge, from Middle English, related to fledge meaning to grow feathers for flight.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the "dg" as a hard "g" sound instead of "j".
Using it for an experienced person who is just new to one job; it implies youth or inexperience in general.

senses.definition: The hair or wool of a sheep or similar animal.
Insulating skin with the wool attached.
A textile similar to velvet, but with a longer pile that gives it a softness and a higher sheen.
An insulating wooly jacket.
Mat or felts composed of fibers, sometimes used as a membrane backer.
Any soft woolly covering resembling a fleece.
The fine web of cotton or wool removed by the doffing knife from the cylinder of a carding machine.
To con or trick (someone) out of money.
To cut off the fleece from (a sheep or other animal).
senses.example: During spring shearing we have to fleece all the sheep in just a few days.

senses.definition: To cover with, or as if with, wool.

core.definition: The thick, woolly coat of a sheep, or a soft, warm fabric made to look or feel like wool.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a long E sound. Keep the final sound clear and crisp, not a soft "z".

nuance.connotation: Neutral for the animal and the fabric; the verb meaning to cheat someone out of money is negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fleece most often for the soft fabric in jackets, blankets and sweatshirts, such as "a fleece jacket". For sheep wool, they say wool or fleece in farming contexts. The verb meaning to cheat someone is more formal or literary and sounds old-fashioned in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Wool is the natural fiber itself; fleece often refers to a knitted or synthetic fabric that imitates wool, such as polyester fleece.
Cheat is the everyday word for dishonesty; fleece specifically means taking large sums from someone who is gullible or inexperienced.

examples.everyday: It's chilly tonight, so grab your fleece before we head out to the game.
examples.professional: Our outdoor team issues a fleece pullover to every field technician, since they work in cold warehouses.
examples.analytical: The scam artists fleeced elderly investors by promising returns that the underlying business could never deliver.

nuance.analogy: Like a soft lamb's coat that you can wear, but synthetic fleece is woven to feel that way without any sheep.
nuance.etymology: From Old English flēos, meaning the woolly coat of a sheep.
common_mistakes: Confusing the noun fleece with the verb's sense of cheating; context matters.
Pronouncing it with a "z" ending instead of a clear "s".

fleece.etymology: From Middle English *fles*, *flees*, *flese*, from Old English *flēos*, *flīes*, *flȳs*, from **fleus*.

senses.definition: In a fleeting manner; transiently.

core.definition: For a very short time; briefly, so that something is seen, felt or noticed only for a moment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, like "fleeting". Keep the "ing" light and end with a clear "-lee".

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly wistful, often used to describe a feeling, expression or image that appears and disappears.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fleetingly mostly in writing and careful speech, especially to describe a look, thought or emotion. In everyday talk people usually say "for a second" or "briefly". It almost always goes with a verb of perception or feeling, such as glimpsed, appeared or crossed.

distinctions.note: Briefly is common and neutral; fleetingly is more literary and suggests something that passes away almost before it is noticed.
Momentarily can also mean temporarily for a short period; fleetingly focuses more on the impression of something passing quickly.

examples.everyday: The thought crossed my mind fleetingly, but I decided it was too silly to say out loud.
examples.professional: The error code appeared fleetingly in the dashboard, so the team could not reproduce it.
examples.analytical: The poem gestures fleetingly toward a divine presence before withdrawing into ordinary speech.

nuance.analogy: Like a bird crossing a window: you catch the movement for an instant before it is gone.
nuance.etymology: From fleeting, the adjective, with the adverbial -ly suffix.
common_mistakes: Using fleetingly for a long, continuous action rather than something brief.
Stressing the second syllable, which makes the word sound foreign.

senses.definition: The water of a flood.

core.definition: Water that spreads over land during a flood, especially water covering fields, streets or homes.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second part, water, has a flapped t and a reduced final er, so it sounds like WAW-der. The ud in flood is a short uh vowel, not oo.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral; it signals danger, loss and damage.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use floodwater mostly in news, weather and disaster contexts, like floodwater rising in the streets. It is a mass noun, so say some floodwater, not a floodwater. In casual talk people often just say the water.

distinctions.note: Flood can mean the event or a great overflow; floodwater is specifically the water itself.
Runoff is rain or snowmelt flowing over the ground toward streams, not necessarily an overflow or a disaster.

examples.everyday: Our basement got soaked with floodwater after the storm last week.
examples.professional: Crews are pumping standing floodwater out of the underpass before inspecting the road.
examples.analytical: The biblical flood narrative describes floodwater covering the earth, a story theologians read as both judgment and new beginning.

nuance.analogy: Like a bathtub that overflows and keeps spreading across the whole floor.
nuance.etymology: From flood (Old English flōd) and water (Old English wæter).
common_mistakes: Saying a floodwater or floodwaters for one event; the mass form is standard.
Writing flood water as two words in formal writing; Americans often write it as one word.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew mabbul (flood, deluge) appears in Genesis 6:17, where God says he will bring a flood of waters upon the earth. Genesis 7:17 says the flood continued forty days upon the earth, with the waters rising until the mountains were covered. Psalm 32:6 says that in the rush of great waters, they shall not reach the godly person who prays.

senses.definition: To incite or cause troublesome acts; to encourage; to instigate.
senses.example: He was arrested for fomenting a riot; after all, it's bad enough being in a riot but starting one is much worse.

senses.definition: To apply a poultice to; to bathe with a cloth or sponge.
Fomentation.

core.definition: To deliberately stir up or encourage trouble, rebellion, or unrest among people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, MENT. The first vowel is a long 'oh,' and do not pronounce the final t as a separate sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative, implying deliberate and often harmful stirring up of conflict.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'foment' mainly in news writing, political commentary, and formal essays, not in casual speech. It almost always has a negative sense of inciting trouble. Everyday speakers are more likely to say 'stir up' or 'cause trouble.' The medical sense of applying a warm compress is rare in American English.

distinctions.note: Incite is more direct and often used for immediate action, while foment suggests slowly building up unrest over time.
Stir up is common and informal, while foment is formal and implies a more calculated effort.

examples.everyday: My uncle loves to foment arguments at family dinners, so I just stay quiet.
examples.professional: The vendor was accused of fomenting panic among our customers with misleading emails.
examples.analytical: Historians argue that the pamphlets did more than report events; they deliberately fomented revolt among the colonists.

nuance.analogy: Like blowing on dying embers until they flare into a fire, fomenting slowly builds unrest into open conflict.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'fomentum' (warm poultice), from 'fovere' (to warm).
common_mistakes: Confusing 'foment' with 'ferment,' which means fermentation or growing agitation without deliberate blame.
Using 'foment' for neutral encouragement; it is almost always negative.

foment.etymology: From Middle English *fomenten*, a borrowing from Old French *fomenter*, from Late Latin *fōmentō*, from Latin *fōmentum* (“lotion”), from *foveō* (“heat, cherish”).

senses.definition: Voluntary choice; (the power of) unforced, uncoerced choice.
senses.example: (insane/worst/best/amazing) use of free will

senses.definition: The ability to choose one's actions and make choices that are not predetermined by predestination, fate, etc.
senses.example: Some people deny that humans have free will, and argue that every thought and action is preordained by God.

core.definition: The ability to make choices that are one's own, not forced or fully determined by outside causes, fate or God.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'free', the first word, as in a compound noun. Keep 'will' short with a clear 'ih' vowel. In writing, 'free will' is two words; the adjective 'free-will' is hyphenated before a noun.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive, linked to dignity and responsibility; it can be contested in philosophy and theology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in everyday conversation and in philosophy and theology. 'Of my own free will' means voluntarily. The debate is between free will and determinism or predestination.

distinctions.note: Determinism claims all events are caused by prior conditions, which seems to leave no room for free will.
Freedom is broader and can mean political liberty, while free will concerns the capacity to choose.
Autonomy means self-governance, often in ethics, while free will is about the power of choice itself.

examples.everyday: Nobody pushed me; I signed up of my own free will.
examples.professional: The consent form must show that participants joined of their own free will.
examples.analytical: Augustine defends free will as the source of sin without making God its author.
